note: Read 2026-11-01 at the owner's word ("Continue on to the rest of layer 4"): the languages each of the map's 252 countries and territories speaks, with each language's share of the population and its official status, from Unicode CLDR 49 (released 2026-10-22), the names of the languages in English, and a scale of how well a language is spoken. One research subagent; every territory's list checked by the lead against the saved CLDR 49 supplementalData.xml (codes written in BCP 47, zh_Hant as zh-Hant). AN (the Netherlands Antilles) and CS (Serbia and Montenegro), dissolved, are not in CLDR 49: AN's last list is CLDR 1.8's (2010), CS has none in any release read. The CEFR's descriptors are read from copies (UHR, DAAD) because coe.int refused this environment.

language population percent — an estimate of the number of people who are functional in that language in that country, including both first and second language speakers. The level of fluency is that necessary to use a UI on a computer, smartphone, or similar devices, rather than complete fluency.

The percentages may add up to more than 100% due to multilingual populations, or may be less than 100% due to illiteracy or because the data has not yet been gathered or processed. Languages with smaller populations might not be included.
official language — as used in CLDR, a language that can generally be used in all communications with a central government.
official regional language — a language that is official ( de jure or de facto ) in a major region within a country, but does not qualify as an official language of the country as a whole.

figures.finding: The CEFR's global scale has six levels in three bands: A1 Breakthrough and A2 Waystage (Basic User), B1 Threshold and B2 Vantage (Independent User), C1 Effective Operational Proficiency and C2 Mastery (Proficient User), each with a short descriptor of what the speaker can do.

cefr.name: Breakthrough
cefr.descriptor: Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type. Can introduce him/herself and others and can ask and answer questions about personal details such as where he/she lives, people he/she knows and things he/she has. Can interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help.

cefr.name: Waystage
cefr.descriptor: Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance (e.g. very basic personal and family information, shopping, local geography, employment). Can communicate in simple and routine tasks requiring a simple and direct exchange of information on familiar and routine matters. Can describe in simple terms aspects of his/her background, immediate environment and matters in areas of immediate need.

cefr.name: Threshold
cefr.descriptor: Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc. Can deal with most situations likely to arise whilst travelling in an area where the language is spoken. Can produce simple connected text on topics which are familiar or of personal interest. Can describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes & ambitions and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans.

cefr.name: Vantage
cefr.descriptor: Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in his/her field of specialisation. Can interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party. Can produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options.

cefr.name: Effective Operational Proficiency
cefr.descriptor: Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning. Can express him/herself fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions. Can use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes. Can produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects, showing controlled use of organisational patterns, connectors and cohesive devices.

cefr.name: Mastery
cefr.descriptor: Can understand with ease virtually everything heard or read. Can summarise information from different spoken and written sources, reconstructing arguments and accounts in a coherent presentation. Can express him/herself spontaneously, very fluently and precisely, differentiating finer shades of meaning even in more complex situations.

value.note: Descriptor text as the UHR copy gives it (CEFR 2001 Table 1 wording); the DAAD copy differs in small words (e.g. C2 'reconstruct' and 'the most complex', C1 'express ideas'); the Council of Europe's own page could not be read from this session.

figures.applies: Any language; the CEFR is the Council of Europe's scale, used across Europe for language tests including naturalisation.
figures.use: Hold each spoken language at a CEFR level A1 to C2 and show the level with its name and first descriptor sentence.

figures.finding: The ILR speaking scale has six base levels, 0 No Proficiency to 5 Functionally Native Proficiency, with plus levels between them.

ilr.name: No Proficiency
ilr.descriptor: Unable to function in the spoken language.

ilr.name: Elementary Proficiency
ilr.descriptor: Able to satisfy minimum courtesy requirements and maintain very simple face-to-face conversations on familiar topics.

ilr.name: Limited Working Proficiency
ilr.descriptor: Able to satisfy routine social demands and limited work requirements.

ilr.name: General Professional Proficiency
ilr.descriptor: Able to speak the language with sufficient structural accuracy and vocabulary to participate effectively in most formal and informal conversations in practical, social and professional topics.

ilr.name: Advanced Professional Proficiency
ilr.descriptor: Able to use the language fluently and accurately on all levels normally pertinent to professional needs.

ilr.name: Functionally Native Proficiency
ilr.descriptor: Speaking proficiency is functionally equivalent to that of a highly articulate well-educated native speaker and reflects the cultural standards of the country where the language is natively spoken.

value.plus_levels: 0+ to 4+ when proficiency substantially exceeds a base level

figures.use: Optional second scale for a US-government part or job that names an ILR rating; the CEFR stays the one the player sees.

sources.said: Speaking 0 (No Proficiency) Unable to function in the spoken language.
Speaking 1 (Elementary Proficiency) Able to satisfy minimum courtesy requirements and maintain very simple face-to-face conversations on familiar topics.
Speaking 2 (Limited Working Proficiency) Able to satisfy routine social demands and limited work requirements.

Speaking 3 (General Professional Proficiency) Able to speak the language with sufficient structural accuracy and vocabulary to participate effectively in most formal and informal conversations in practical, social and professional topics.
Speaking 4 (Advanced Professional Proficiency) Able to use the language fluently and accurately on all levels normally pertinent to professional needs.

Speaking 5 (Functionally Native Proficiency) Speaking proficiency is functionally equivalent to that of a highly articulate well-educated native speaker and reflects the cultural standards of the country where the language is natively spoken.
The "plus level" designation (coded 06, 16, 26, etc.) will be assigned when proficiency substantially exceeds one base skill level and does not fully meet the criteria for the next "base level."
